sections.title: What is Basic Math for CP?
sections.content:
Mathematics is not optional in competitive programming - it is a constant companion. Almost every non-trivial problem touches number theory, combinatorics, or arithmetic in some way. The question is whether you have the right tools ready or whether you get stuck re-deriving them under time pressure.

**Modular arithmetic** appears whenever answers get large. Problems say 'output the answer modulo 10^9+7' because the actual answer can be astronomically large - bigger than any integer type can hold. Understanding mod is not just a formatting requirement; it changes how you compute intermediate values.

**GCD and LCM** appear in fraction problems, problems asking about common divisors, period/cycle detection, and more. The Euclidean algorithm is one of the oldest algorithms in existence and is still the tool you reach for here.

**Prime numbers** appear in factorization problems, cryptography-adjacent problems, and anytime the structure of a number's divisors matters. Knowing when to use trial division versus a sieve is a practical skill.

**Combinatorics** - counting arrangements and selections - appears in probability problems, DP state counting, and 'count the number of ways' problems. The factorial grows faster than almost anything, so you need to know how to compute binomial coefficients without overflow.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: Pull from this toolkit whenever a problem involves counting, divisibility, large number arithmetic, or asks about prime factors. The phrase 'modulo 10^9+7' in the output specification is the clearest signal that modular arithmetic is required. 'How many ways' signals combinatorics. 'Divisible by', 'common divisor', or 'reduce the fraction' signals GCD/LCM.
signals: prime factorization / prime numbers up to n
how many pairs satisfy a condition
reduce a fraction to lowest terms
power of a number modulo m

sections.title: Modular Arithmetic
GCD and LCM
sections.content:
The **Greatest Common Divisor** (GCD) of two numbers is the largest number that divides both. The **Euclidean algorithm** computes it efficiently using one key insight: `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b)`. This works because any divisor of both `a` and `b` also divides `a % b`.

Base case: `gcd(a, 0) = a`.

```javascript
function gcd(a, b) {
  return b === 0 ? a : gcd(b, a % b);
}
```

The number of recursive calls is O(log(min(a, b))) - the remainder shrinks by at least half every two steps.

## LCM from GCD

`lcm(a, b) = (a / gcd(a, b)) * b`

Divide before multiplying to avoid overflow: `(a / gcd(a, b)) * b` rather than `(a * b) / gcd(a, b)`.

sections.title: Primes
Combinatorics Basics
sections.content:
**Combinatorics** counts arrangements and selections. The core operation is **nCr** (n choose r): the number of ways to choose `r` items from `n` items without regard to order.

`nCr = n! / (r! * (n-r)!)`

## Pascal's Triangle

Pascal's triangle gives nCr values without computing factorials directly. Each cell is the sum of the two above it: `C(n, r) = C(n-1, r-1) + C(n-1, r)`. This is an O(n²) precomputation that answers any nCr query in O(1).

## Factorial Overflow

`20!` overflows a 64-bit integer. For large `n`, compute nCr modulo a prime `p` using: `nCr % p = n! * modInverse(r!) * modInverse((n-r)!) % p`. This requires modular inverse (Fermat's little theorem: `modInverse(a, p) = modPow(a, p-2, p)` when `p` is prime).

sections.title: Core Template
sections.explanation: These are the five functions you'll copy into nearly every math-heavy CP solution. GCD/LCM handle divisibility, modPow handles large exponentiation without overflow, modInverse enables modular division, and safeMod handles JavaScript's negative remainder quirk.

items.name: Extended Euclidean Algorithm (Modular Inverse)
items.description: The extended Euclidean algorithm finds integers `x, y` such that `ax + by = gcd(a, b)`. When `gcd(a, m) = 1`, this gives `ax ≡ 1 (mod m)`, making `x` the modular inverse of `a`. This works for any modulus, not just primes, unlike the Fermat's little theorem approach.

items.name: Chinese Remainder Theorem
items.description: CRT solves systems of simultaneous modular equations: find `x` such that `x ≡ r1 (mod m1)`, `x ≡ r2 (mod m2)`, etc., when all moduli are coprime. It appears in problems with multiple periodic conditions. Too advanced for Level 0 but worth knowing exists.

items.name: Segmented Sieve
items.description: When you need primes in a range [L, R] where R is large (up to 10^12) but the range R - L is manageable (≤ 10^6), the segmented sieve uses the base sieve up to √R and marks composites in the target range only. Dramatically reduces memory.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.time: O(√n) trial division, O(n log log n) sieve, O(log n) GCD, O(log exp) modPow
sections.space: O(n) for sieve, O(log n) recursion stack for GCD
sections.explanation: Trial division is O(√n) because we only test factors up to the square root. The sieve is O(n log log n) because each prime p marks n/p composites, and the sum of 1/p for all primes up to n converges to log log n. GCD is O(log(min(a,b))) because the remainder shrinks by at least half every two steps - matching binary search's halving behavior.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: JS integer overflow with large products: `a * b` where both are around 10^9 silently gives a wrong float result. Use BigInt for intermediate products before taking mod, or restructure to mod earlier: `(a % mod) * (b % mod) % mod` still risks overflow for mod near 10^9 - use BigInt.

Negative modulo in JS: `(-1 % 5)` returns `-1` in JavaScript, not `4`. Whenever you subtract and take mod, use `((n % m) + m) % m` to guarantee a non-negative result. Forgetting this causes wrong answers on problems with subtraction.
Treating 1 as prime: 1 has only one divisor (itself), not two, so by definition it is not prime. Including 1 in a prime list corrupts sieve results and breaks factorization logic.
Trial division running to n instead of √n: looping `for (let i = 2; i <= n; i++)` to check primality is O(n) and will TLE for n up to 10^9. Always loop to `i * i <= n` or precompute `Math.sqrt(n)`.
Starting inner sieve loop at 2*i instead of i*i: multiples of `i` smaller than `i*i` were already marked by smaller primes. Starting at `i*i` is both correct and faster.

items.title: Count Primes
items.why: Direct application of the Sieve of Eratosthenes - tests whether you know the O(n log log n) algorithm versus O(n√n) naive.

items.title: Palindrome Number
items.why: Tests digit extraction using modulo and integer division - the most fundamental mod operations.

items.title: Reverse Integer
items.why: Combines digit extraction with overflow detection - tests whether you understand integer limits and safe mod arithmetic.

items.title: Add Digits
items.why: Tests recognition of digital root formula - rewards knowing the mod 9 mathematical pattern over iterative simulation.

sections.title: What to Learn Next
sections.why: Loops are the mechanical tool that executes the mathematical ideas you just learned - sieve loops, modPow loops, and digit extraction loops all require fluency with loop bounds and nested iteration.
